rail_guard.text: Waverley Station, the only station in the world named after a novel. It's named after Sir Walter Scott's 'Waverley'. The trains are not obliged to be as long.
Hop aboard! The Wildlore rail runs to every station you've visited in Great Britain. Where to?

then.text: There's a ceilidh tonight. I'm told I dance like a shopping trolley with a wonky wheel. I've been practising on the cobbles. The pigeons are unimpressed.
You go on ahead. I'll catch you up. Probably. If there's a scone.
The Castle Esplanade: cobbles, a crowd, and the Castle itself standing on its black rock like a very old cat on a very tall fence. Kit is sitting on a bollard eating chips with a wooden fork.
{player}! Edinburgh Castle! I've been up and down the Royal Mile three times. My legs have filed a complaint.
How many Stones is that now? Eight? I've got... fewer. Typical. One more go, for old times' sake?

else.text: I'll tell you what, though. Standing up here, looking out at the whole city, I remembered why I started. Not the likes. Just the walking.
Strachan's up in the Highlands, apparently. Waxed jacket, clipboard. She has a lanyard that makes Kerrigan's look casual. Be careful.

then.text: Haar's in! The Castle's up there somewhere, I promise. Use your imagination, it's included in the tour.
A wee bit of rain makes the Old Town look its spooky best. Umbrellas up, everyone, follow the brolly.
Last tour of the day, and the closes get shadowy now. Stick close. The ghosts like stragglers.

edi_guide.text: The Castle's on a volcanic plug. A big old volcano chilled out about 340 million years ago, and the glaciers scraped it into a crag with a long tail. Hence 'Crag and Tail'.
The One O'Clock Gun goes off at one o'clock. It started in 1861 so ships in the Forth could set their clocks. Now it startles tourists. A fine tradition.

then.text: Good hat. I'd put you on a poster. Terms and conditions apply.
Burns Night! Haggis, neeps and tatties, and a man in the corner reciting all of Tam o' Shanter whether you like it or not.
Up here it's guising, not trick or treating. You tell a joke, you get a sweetie. My best one got me a satsuma.
Christmas is just the warm-up act. Hogmanay's the main event.
The Fringe is long gone and I'm still doing my show. Audience of one. It's that pigeon again.
Rain's great for comedy. Everyone ducks into a show to dry off, and suddenly I've got an audience. Of six.
I tried flyering on the Royal Mile in this wind. My flyers are now somewhere over Fife, doing very well.
Just finished my late show. Nine people came. Three laughed. One was my mum, but she still counts.

edi_fringe.text: {greeting} In August the Fringe takes over the whole city: thousands of shows, a few hundred of them with real audiences, and one with a very committed accordion.
It's the biggest arts festival in the world. I'm doing a comedy set about pigeons. It's called 'Squab Goes Hungry'. Come on Tuesday. There'll be a seat.

then.text: Lovely day for the Gardens. The Floral Clock's ticking nicely and so are my knees, unfortunately.
Free watering from above. I'll take it. The flowers love it and I get a sit down in the shed.

edi_gardener.text: The Floral Clock's a proper working clock and, I'll have you know, the oldest in the world. It's all planted in spring. It takes a month and a lot of kneeling.
Mind the daffs. Children can walk on the daffs, but only after school.

then.text: Burns Night. You address the haggis like a guest of honour, then you stab it. Very Scottish hospitality.
Arthur's Seat in a frost. Cracking view. Can't feel my ears.
I wouldn't climb Arthur's Seat in this wind. You'd go up a walker and come down a kite.
Grand day for a climb. From the top you can see right over the Forth to Fife. Fife waves back, mostly.
Up early to catch the sunrise from the hill. The skylarks beat me to it. They always do.

edi_walker.text: {greeting} Arthur's Seat is an extinct volcano with a nice view and a path. You can be on top of it in an hour, and you will want a scone afterwards.
They say King Arthur sat there, but there's no real evidence. There's a lot of evidence for seagulls.

edinburgh_lamplighter.text: There's still a few gas lamps in the New Town. Someone's got to keep them glowing, and tonight that's me.
Robert Louis Stevenson watched the lamplighter from his window as a boy, and wrote a poem about it. No pressure.
Quiet streets, warm lamps, cobbles shining. Edinburgh at night is like walking through a storybook.

edinburgh_astronomer.text: There's an old observatory up on Calton Hill. The city lights get in the way now, but the Moon doesn't mind.
See that wee fuzzy patch? That's the Orion Nebula, where new stars are born. Like a nursery, but hotter.
Most folk look down at the city from up here. I look the other way. Better view, fewer seagulls.
